title: We Agreed to divorce, Yet You Hold Me Every Night
author: Happy Pearl
synopsis:
Lu Huaixi had been slipped onto the list of girls entering the imperial palace. Left with no good options, she got engaged to Xie Yuanjing — a man she had absolutely nothing to do with. A one-year agreement. Each getting what they need. After the separation, their marriages would be none of each other's business. Lu Huaixi was perfectly satisfied with this.

But Xie Yuanjing seemed a little *too* good to her — and she found herself sinking in, just a tiny bit.

Xie Yuanjing brought home a young girl and treated her like a child to look after — proper and upright, letting her do as she pleased. But the girl was too good. He sank in. He couldn't stand to see her grow close to others, couldn't stand to see her smile at someone else, couldn't stand to see her distance herself from him. He wanted to trade everything good he had just to make her stay.

Later, when the Lu family patriarch was wondering where his daughter could go after the separation, Young Master Xie pulled her back behind him.

"Separation? There's no such thing."

chapters.title: Not Wanting to Become a Nun
chapters.content:
"Shu Mama has brought new portraits of eligible young men. If you still can't choose one, you might as well shave your head and become a nun."

In the front hall, a young man frowned as he flipped through a stack of portraits, his voice laced with impatience—yet he was scrutinizing each one more carefully than the person they were meant for, finding every candidate more unsatisfactory than the last.

Across from him, a girl who had just come of age leaned her cheek against her hand, her hair pinned up in a lively and playful style, though her eyes were heavy with drowsiness.

"I don't want to become a nun. The mountains are too cold, and you can't eat whatever you like."

"Still thinking about eating? If your marriage isn't settled this month, your only choices are the mountains or the palace. Given your 'brilliance,' the first might let you scrape by—the second would be a slow death sentence."

Having been scolded by her own brother, the girl finally sat up straight.

She lowered her head reluctantly and reached over to pull out one of the scrolls, unrolling it.

"This one won't do—his household has too many concubines."

She set it aside and picked up the next.

The young man glanced over and declined on her behalf without even looking up.

"This one is a decent scholar. His family background is modest, but with some support his future would be secure. The only question is whether he'd want to marry someone like you who despises reading."

"This one—forget it. There were rumors recently that he's been keeping a mistress. Even if you became his primary wife, you'd never hold sway over him."

"This one..."

One by one, the portraits were set aside. In the end, only four thin scrolls remained.

The man depicted in the topmost portrait had a thick, blade-like beard and a powerfully built frame. He looked nothing like a young man who had barely come of age—he appeared as someone who had endured years of rigorous training, fierce and imposing.

The siblings' eyes landed on the portrait simultaneously, and both fell silent for a moment.

"Brother, honestly—even if I were sent to the palace, I might not necessarily be selected, right?"

Silence fell over the front hall. No one answered.

The girl slumped her head in dismay.

In the Great Yu dynasty, participation in the imperial selection was not compulsory. But recently, a piece of news had surfaced—someone had placed her name, Lu Huaixi, on the Flower and Bird Envoy's list.

And along with the listing, her habits, mannerisms, and even her portrait had been submitted.

Such swiftness could only mean someone had been pulling strings behind the scenes.

But her elder brother, Lu Yuanzhao, would not say any of this to her.

He couldn't bring himself to tell her the truth: that just by virtue of being from the Lu family, the one in the palace could never afford to let her go.

Let alone the fact that Lu Huaixi was beautiful—her looks were like flowers in bloom, and with her lazy, sun-warmed charm and endearing sweetness, she was the kind of face that made hearts stir.

"Stop brooding. Look through the rest. As for this... this robust warrior—what do you think?"

Lu Huaixi looked up at her brother in surprise, her lips parting slightly. In the end, she swallowed whatever fear she'd been about to voice.

Smoothly, the portrait was turned to the next one.

But a moment later, Lu Yuanzhao glanced sideways at his sister and frowned.

"He Jian Hang—no. The He family has too much ambition, and this youngest son of theirs has eyes bigger than his stomach. Don't let him fool you."

As he finished speaking, Lu Yuanzhao's expression darkened of its own accord.

He had suddenly realized that the high-born young lords and scions of noble houses all harbored their share of shameful secrets.

Hearing about their dalliances in passing was one thing, but the moment any of it touched his sister, it was the kind of thing that could come to blows at any moment.

And that was to say nothing of the fact that the He family and the Lu family were now political rivals.

From neighbors and close friends to bitter enemies—that transformation had taken no more than a year.

Lu Huaixi blinked and said nothing.

In the quiet, the final two portraits were laid flat on the table together.

Lu Huaixi's gaze dropped to them, and for a moment, it stilled.

One was Zhao Luo—she vaguely recognized him, though they had never had much dealings.

And the other—

Lu Huaixi's gaze settled on the man's cool and naturally handsome face. Though it was only an inked rendering, the likeness still made her pause for a heartbeat when she first saw it.

"He—how did he end up in here?"

The young lord of the Chengen Marquis' household—Xie Yuanjing, the late empress' own nephew.

This man's looks were extraordinary. Both his features and his bearing were of the rarest beauty, yet his temperament was difficult to read.

Occasionally he smiled at people, but always with an undercurrent of cool detachment that never quite disappeared.

Lu Huaixi's words came out a little stuttery, as if she could see through the portrait to that moment when he had laid hands on someone.

"Isn't he that terrifying Xie Yuanjing?"

"I don't know either."

Lu Yuanzhao spoke, then hesitated for a moment.

"If nothing had gone wrong for the Chengen Marquis' household, Father would never have dared consider him. Actually, even with what happened, Father probably wouldn't want to get entangled with him either. The portrait must have been included by mistake."

Xie Yuanjing was ruthless and yet oddly principled, possessing the calculating approach of the old guard while striking with the speed and precision of the young.

Though Lu Yuanzhao had always believed the Chengen Marquis' household would regain its power under Xie Yuanjing's hand, he had absolutely no desire to get on his good side.

This man's mind ran too deep—he couldn't fathom it.

But one thing he was certain of: Xie Yuanjing would never allow himself to be distracted by marriage matters at a time when the marquis' household needed to make its comeback.

"He's out of the question—you don't even need to think about it, he's clearly not suitable—"

"Young Master, Second Young Miss."

Before he could finish, Shu Mama entered from outside, her expression carrying a trace of displeasure, her sharp eyes pressing down some concealed indignation.

"What is it, Shu Mama?"

Both siblings looked over.

Shu Mama met Lu Huaixi's lovely gaze, startled for a moment, then pressed her emotions back down and smiled at her.

"Nothing, nothing. It's just this old servant's poor memory—I forgot to remove a few portraits of young men who are already engaged. I only just remembered."

The explanation came smoothly. Lu Huaixi's lips parted in surprise, but she obediently closed them again.

Lu Yuanzhao's expression shifted.

An obvious excuse, easy enough to see through—someone must have let slip some news from the palace. Several families who had initially shown interest, upon hearing something, no longer dared to get involved, and turned their consideration elsewhere.

Quickly, Shu Mama took away several portraits.

Most of those that remained carried an air of frivolity.

The ones of high status were unwilling to marry into it; the ones of low status didn't dare. The matter ground to a halt somewhere in the middle.

In the whole front hall, only Lu Huaixi showed no sign of distress.

She had returned to her original languorous drowsiness, her fair and delicate hand propped lightly against one cheek, her long curled lashes drooping downward, her fingertips idly toying with the portraits on the table.

It seemed she was resigned to becoming a nun—but she really didn't want that.

The girl sighed, her unfocused gaze drifting at last to Xie Yuanjing's portrait, her wandering fingertip coming to rest on his flat, straight lips.

Thin lips. That must mean he's heartless.

Lost in thought, a small stir arose from outside the courtyard, followed by someone hurrying by, lowering their voice to instruct another.

"An honored guest has arrived at the mansion—hurry and go brew tea."

Lu Yuanzhao rose to his feet, his handsome brow faintly creased. He was about to ask what was happening when he looked up and saw his father returning home, engaged in conversation with someone across the courtyard.

And beside him—a flash of black.

A man of clean, upright bearing stood out unmistakably.

The surprise lasted only a moment before the visitors stepped into the front hall.

Lu's father noticed that both of his children were present—one standing there in a daze, the other impossible to read, whether lazy or drowsy, blinking with a vague, unfocused air. His brow twitched.

"Why aren't you back in your own courtyard? What are you two doing here?"

Lu's father naturally noticed the things laid out on the table.

He hadn't expected that his two children would be sitting there without a care in the world, boldly looking through marriage portraits right under everyone's noses. His head was starting to ache.

"Please don't laugh at us, Lord Xie."

"I arrived without notice."

The man's voice was somewhat low. He ignored Lu's father's hand gesturing behind his back for everyone to leave, and with an easygoing smile, he nodded amiably at the motionless Lu Yuanzhao.

But the smile was faint, a fleeting thing, like a perfunctory courtesy—languid and offhand.

Then his gaze swept past Lu Yuanzhao to what lay behind him.

After one glance at Lu Huaixi, the man's eyes dropped slightly at their outer corners, his gaze coming to rest on her fingertip—on his own portrait.

chapters.title: Xie Yuanjing Is Not Suitable
chapters.content:
Lu Huaixi didn't register it at first. She stared at the flesh-and-blood person before her, momentarily dumbstruck.

The ink had captured Xie Yuanjing's likeness with perhaps seventy percent accuracy. The brushstrokes at the outer corners of his eyes had left a faint touch of red, the subtle upward tilt lending a warmth to what was otherwise an inky, cold, and sharp gaze.

But even with such a beautiful portrait, it still fell short of the man himself by half.

Lu Yuanzhao was the first to come to his senses. He gave a light cough, then turned to give Lu Huaixi a look over his shoulder, wordlessly signaling her to clear the table.

Only then did Lu Huaixi remember—before this man had walked in, she had been studying him with the express purpose of sizing him up as a potential husband.

And it hadn't only been him. She'd looked at many others.

A sudden flush of heat crept up her face. Realizing how mortifying this was, Lu Huaixi shot to her feet, leaned forward to cover the table, and—in a completely futile attempt at concealment—shoved the portraits to the side.

She had just barely managed to block the face on Xie Yuanjing's portrait when the man smiled again.

"Second Young Miss Lu."

He had called to her, yet said nothing more—as if simply offering a greeting.

But he had just seen his own portrait laid out on the table. So when that address fell on Lu Huaixi's ears, it carried an inexplicable weight of deeper meaning.

On the small path leading toward the inner gate, Lu Huaixi still hadn't fully recovered from the earlier awkwardness.

She generally wasn't prone to temper, and her manner of speaking was soft and unhurried. Even now, if she tried to put on a fierce front, the fierceness in it wouldn't hold a candle to the new puppy someone had just brought into the courtyard.

Beside a resting pavilion stood a sweet osmanthus tree, and the two siblings stopped beneath it.

Lu Huaixi, ears still red, shoved the hastily gathered portraits into her maid's arms all at once, then glared at her brother.

"I told you I wanted to look at these in my own courtyard, but you insisted it was too hot to move!"

Lu Yuanzhao touched his nose.

For once, the usually sharp-tongued young man could find no words to argue back. He could only sort through what he wanted to say and pick a few lines.

"Don't worry. Xie Yuanjing would never bring this up on his own. He's a crafty old fox in disguise—even if a portrait of himself ends up in someone else's hands for inspection, he'd only ever act as though nothing happened. He wouldn't embarrass either family."

Lu Huaixi's indignation, which had been simmering a moment ago, deflated all at once along with her brow.

"Why was his portrait in there anyway?"

"No idea. Either way, it certainly wasn't his own idea."

With that confirmed and out of the question, Lu Huaixi relaxed somewhat—though she still let out a dejected sigh.

"But then what am I supposed to do? Out of all those portraits, his was the only good-looking one."

"...What do you mean? Did you take a liking to—no, don't even think about it."

Lu Yuanzhao mercilessly pierced through her little daydream. "Xie Yuanjing could never give his heart to marriage matters. Even back when he was riding high, he never showed any intention of settling down. Now—even less so."

"Oh."

Lu Huaixi pursed her lips.

This was really so annoying.

She didn't want to become a nun, and she didn't want to wait for death. Why did her brother have to say it with such finality?

"Actually, my luck is usually pretty decent. Even the abbot at Wénan Temple once said my fate has an unusual quality—I always end up with a little more good fortune than ordinary people. So what if—"

"What if you catch the eye of a young, talented gentleman of good character and passable looks? That's quite possible. But if that person is Xie Yuanjing, then it's absolutely out of the question."

Lu Yuanzhao cut her off.

"Give it up. Your fate and Xie Yuanjing's have no business crossing. And do you really think there's no one in the Chengen Marquis' household already pining for him? If even the moon right next to his window is out of reach, what makes you think someone on the outside has a shot?"

Lu Huaixi's curiosity had been piqued and she was about to ask who in the marquis' household had her eye on him, when the branches overhead suddenly rustled.

Birds chirped—several at once, gathering together.

The two siblings had just started to look up when several white specks came dropping from between the leaves.

They were aimed right at the gap between the siblings' overlapping sleeves, yet in the end, they landed with perfect precision on the cuff of Lu Yuanzhao's sleeve.

Missing Lu Huaixi by just an inch.

Watching her brother's expression crumple, Lu Huaixi's earlier unhappiness vanished in an instant.

"Quite the 'extra little good fortune' you've got there."

Lu Yuanzhao gritted his teeth, forcing himself to swallow his revulsion. "I'm going to change. You—get back to your own courtyard and stay there!"

Lu Huaixi couldn't hold back her laughter. She waved him off with eyes curved into crescent moons, watching her brother storm away.

In the front hall, a cup of hot tea was carefully set down before Xie Yuanjing.

Spring was drawing to a close. The days still carried some cool freshness after rain, but most of the time they came with heat.

Xie Yuanjing glanced down at the steam curling above the tea surface without reaching for it.

Lu Yandao had spent twenty-seven years in officialdom and had sharp eyes. Even so, he still found the young lord of the marquis' household somewhat difficult to read.

But he understood clearly that no matter how fallen the Chengen Marquis' household had become, the young man before him was not someone to be trifled with carelessly.

"Today's incident may be a misunderstanding. I hope Lord Xie will not take it to heart."

Lu Yandao's words were deliberately vague, but both men understood: he was referring to the matter of the portrait.

Xie Yuanjing's expression was blank, his demeanor unhurried.

Just as Lu Yandao began to think the man had no intention of discussing such things, Xie Yuanjing suddenly smiled.

"The grand selection is in the eighth month."

His tone was calm and offhand, as if commenting on the weather. "If a marriage engagement is settled too late, it may appear as deliberate evasion—a slight against His Majesty's wishes."

At that, even Lu Yandao—practiced as he was at keeping his emotions in check—couldn't help a trace of worry from surfacing.

But in order to avoid the palace by marrying off his daughter, a matter that could at any moment be seized upon as a handle against him, he absolutely could not let anything slip to another person.

"Lord Xie misunderstands. Our dynasty has never compelled the daughters of officials into the selection. My daughter's portrait viewing is simply a matter of a father wishing to plan ahead for her future. You must be laughing at me."

"Is that so."

Xie Yuanjing nodded, unhurried. "Then it seems I was misinformed."

Every shift in Lu Yandao's expression had fallen under Xie Yuanjing's gaze. His own face remained unreadable, yet inwardly he added a few more strokes to his impression of Lu Huaixi.

Deeply valued. Acceptable.

"Since it is a misunderstanding, let us not speak of it further."

Xie Yuanjing said no more on the matter, but Lu Yandao steered the conversation back.

"Even so—Lord Xie mentioned being misinformed. What did you mean by that?"

"Nothing of great consequence. Only that I had heard someone placed Second Young Miss Lu on the Flower and Bird Envoy's list, and I assumed Lord Lu was troubled by the matter."

"That piece of news—"

Lu Yandao was indeed troubled. But what truly alarmed him was that the information had somehow reached the ears of the man before him.

He pressed down his thoughts, not wishing to reveal too much.

"What a preposterous thing."

Lu Yandao frowned. "Then Lord Xie came today to offer a word of caution?"

"No. I came to put myself forward."

"What?"

"To speak of a marriage arrangement. I am, I believe, a suitable match."

When there was no conflict between them, Xie Yuanjing's manner toward others was naturally languid and indifferent.

Even when speaking of something as weighty as a marriage proposal, the words came from his mouth as casually as a passing remark about the day's weather.

"Of course—on the condition that Second Young Miss Lu is willing."

chapters.title: Never Mind if She Has Someone She Likes
chapters.content:
"Is that so."

Xie Yuanjing smiled slightly, the outer corners of his eyes lifting just a fraction. The cold air that usually surrounded him softened, replaced by something more measured and calm.

"But I appear to be the only one who can help Second Young Miss."

He said it unhurriedly. "I have my own aims in this. If Lord Lu agrees, I can prevent the Second Young Miss from entering the palace—and I can guarantee that after the wedding, while I attend to her needs, I will not harbor any romantic intentions toward her."

"One year after the wedding, I will sign the dissolution of marriage and give her her freedom. After that, should she wish to remarry, I will always be her support—without exception."

"I have no wish to speak in circles with Lord Lu. To put it plainly: I just saw Second Young Miss holding my portrait, and I believe this match is, in fact, quite suitable."

Lu Yandao was so infuriated his expression crumpled.

His gaze sharpened in an instant, carrying the weight and displeasure of a man accustomed to authority.

"Lord Xie may treat marriage as child's play—whether you use people or not is your own affair. But my daughter will never be anyone's pawn."

"A pawn... does Lord Lu truly believe that arranging a hasty engagement for Second Young Miss now will secure her a good husband?"

The corner of Xie Yuanjing's mouth curved with a fleeting mockery.

"Rushing her into marriage with some random man before the grand selection is what's child's play. No matter how capable the Lu family is, a daughter married off in a hurry will always be looked down upon—and there's nothing to be done about it later. But with me, it's different—"

Xie Yuanjing spoke of his purpose without the slightest concealment, frank and unabashed.

On the table, the tea was gradually cooling. Once the heat faded and the steam dispersed, the clear surface lay undisturbed.

Only then did Xie Yuanjing reach for the cup.

He took a sip and continued at his own unhurried pace:

"I have my purpose. Therefore, before the dissolution, I will give Second Young Miss every respect I am capable of giving, and I have no interest in affairs of the heart. Once things have settled, whenever she wishes to leave, I will accommodate her."

The hall fell momentarily silent, broken only by the soft clink of the teacup being set back on the table.

Xie Yuanjing did not press for an answer and made no move to ask for one. He simply rose to his feet, and before taking his leave, produced a jade pendant.

The red cord was somewhat aged, worn with the passage of years.

"This belongs to the elder of my household. Upon learning I was visiting the Lu residence today, he entrusted me to bring it to Lord Lu's honored grandfather."

The close friendship between the two families had been severed in their parents' generation; the younger heirs had had no dealings since. Yet Lu Yandao still held scattered memories of those days.

At the sight of this jade pendant with its intimate and personal air, a sense of foreboding stirred within him—though he gave nothing away on his face.

"Lord Xie mentioned having a purpose. You might as well say it plainly."

"There's no hurry."

Xie Yuanjing smiled without much concern. "What matters more right now is Second Young Miss's own feelings. In the end it was I who came without invitation—if she's willing to consider it, there will be time enough to speak of it then."

chapters.title: Are You Willing to Consider It? This Marriage Arrangement
chapters.content:
Lu Huaixi had not been taken in by He Jianxing's talk—but his words had, unexpectedly, planted a rare seed of heaviness in her heart.

In the past few days, neither her father nor her mother had spoken to her in detail about the matter. Her brother always brought it up in a teasing, joking way, as if trying to soften the blow of what lay ahead.

But it wasn't as though she didn't know.

More than that, what concerned Lu Huaixi most at this moment was not the matter itself—it was the fact that what had started as rumor had already spread outside.

Someone must have been using public opinion to block any path she might have of escaping the selection through marriage.

If that was the case, then the men in those portraits were even less likely to be willing to wade into such murky waters.

Lu Huaixi was troubled, no longer in any mood to listen to He Jianxing's ramblings.

She was about to make herself clear and looked up—only to meet a gaze impossible to ignore.

Also from a carriage.

Not far away, the carriage curtain had been lifted halfway. Xie Yuanjing sat inside. The man's dark clothing carried a cool edge about it, his handsome face half-shadowed in dim light.

Lu Huaixi couldn't quite make out his eyes from where she stood, yet she could feel with certainty that he was watching her—a gaze as still and deep as the bottom of a lake, quiet yet pressing.

"Huaixi, if Lord Lu takes your side in helping me, once I've found my footing I'll make sure to protect you well. Even if Father disapproves, I'll do everything in my power—for your sake—"

"No thank you. I have no interest in someone who's already been betrothed—and you are not to my taste."

Lu Huaixi cut him off, as straightforward as ever.

She hadn't meant to humiliate him. There was impatience in her, yes, but her eyes remained guileless and steady.

Once she had finished, she looked again toward that carriage not far away.

Still there. Strange.

Xie Yuanjing, watching from the carriage, had not lowered his curtain. He had a perfectly clear view of Lu Huaixi's face and its parade of expressions.

There were plenty in the capital who had talked about the Lu family's second daughter, yet calling her a "beautiful simpleton" still showed they were being too kind.

If anything, a girl like Lu Huaixi—who couldn't compose poetry, couldn't paint, who'd been raised in indulgence and loved nothing but idle play—would typically be called a fool wrapped in a pretty face.

Perhaps because Xie Yuanjing had been watching for a while, the man beside him shifted slightly and followed his gaze—but quickly sat back again, making no move to let himself be seen.

"You think the Lu family will agree? I have a feeling the Lu family can barely keep peace among themselves. Would Lu the Elder really want to wade into your muddy waters?"

The business of Lu Huaixi being pushed onto the Flower and Bird Envoy's list was suspicious no matter how you looked at it.

And apart from the Lu family's own people, no one else would know Lu Huaixi well enough to pick out exactly the qualities that would catch someone's eye.

"I don't know."

Xie Yuanjing pulled the corner of his mouth into a brief curve. "But it doesn't matter. Lu Huaixi agreeing is what counts."

"You said just now that if she had someone she liked, you'd leave it alone?"

"Mm. But it's not certain yet. Before conviction, one should first see the confession."

The carriage in front of Lu Huaixi finally began to move. As the curtain fell, Xie Yuanjing caught one last fleeting glimpse of the face inside.

It wasn't the sort of face worth remembering—ordinary, coarse, and wearing the raw sulking of someone with no real power.

If that was the taste Lu Huaixi had in men, then he wouldn't wait for the Lu family to decline. He would be the first to change his mind.

"Hey—where are you going?"

Xie Yuanjing didn't answer. He simply leaned forward slightly and, with a slender hand, lifted the hanging curtain at the front of the carriage.

The black boot embroidered with golden cloud motifs touched down on the ground. The man straightened, his refined features falling into full view without obstruction.

Then he walked forward, steps steady and unhurried.

Lu Huaixi had only just studied his portrait under the guise of sizing up a potential match—pretending she hadn't seen him now would be rather awkward.

"Lord Xie."

"Was that person just now an acquaintance of Second Young Miss?"

"No."

Lu Huaixi shook her head. He Jianxing had indeed liked to hover around her before the two families fell out, but once the rift formed, no one had made a bigger show of cutting ties than him.

She could never make a friend of someone like that.

"Not close."

"Was he in that stack of portraits?"

"Ah? Oh."

Xie Yuanjing took in the slight blankness in her expression and guessed it as a yes. He gave a measured nod.

"Then has Second Young Miss made her choice?"

He said, "From those portraits—did you find someone suitable?"

"Not... yet."

"Is that so. So—no one appealed to you?"

Xie Yuanjing's voice had a faint lilt at the end, as if tinged with gentle regret. Then he lowered his eyes and said nothing.

Lu Huaixi couldn't decipher his meaning, and only blinked at him.

At last she remembered the expression on this man's face when he'd noticed the portrait in the front hall. After a moment's hesitation, she decided to speak first.

"I don't know why Lord Xie's portrait ended up in there, but please be at ease—today was purely an accident."

"Second Young Miss hasn't answered me yet."

"What?"

"The men in the portraits—none of them were to your liking?"

Xie Yuanjing was undeniably the kind of person who made others uneasy.

Even with that barely-there smile at the corner of his mouth, he didn't look like someone easy to deal with.

Lu Huaixi was not particularly timid as a rule. If her brother hadn't flatly shut the door on Xie Yuanjing as a possibility so many times, she might have followed his lead and said something like, "Actually, I think I saw someone I liked."

But right now her heart was weighted with something heavy, and this man before her seemed like someone from an entirely different world.

Better not to say it.

"Not exactly—but, all the same, none of them were truly suitable."

The sun was fierce that day, and the longer it beat down, the more the ground grew warm underfoot.

Lu Huaixi was only standing in half-shade, yet a faint flush had already spread across her face, blooming naturally against her fair and delicate skin.

No powder, no rouge—and still lovely. More catching to the eye than all the spring light spread across the hills.

Xie Yuanjing's gaze passed over her downcast lashes, then lingered on the slightly drooping outer corners of her eyes—where she looked listless and a little dejected.

The girl still carried a childlike quality, the kind that came from being wholly sheltered. Her grievances and unhappiness were never really hidden.

"There's nothing unsuitable about it."

Xie Yuanjing replied, tone easy, as though he saw nothing odd at all about asking.

"Is there someone you have feelings for?"

"...No."

"Someone else you'd like to marry?"

"No one."

"Mm."

He gave a nod. Then, shifting course entirely: "The portrait may have been an accident. But now that it has come into Second Young Miss's hands, you are welcome to consider me."

Lu Huaixi looked up, a little startled.

"You may consider me as a prospective husband. I can help you avoid this year's grand selection."

"Help?"

"Yes. Help."

Xie Yuanjing did not elaborate, but the sharpness of the person before him prompted him to speak plainly.

"Second Young Miss will inevitably lose something over this selection. But I may be able to minimize that loss."

As he spoke, Xie Yuanjing's gaze remained fixed on Lu Huaixi's face.

Her eyes were very clear. Even when touched with emotion, they never tried to hide anything—they simply held whatever they felt, openly.

Very easy to read.

Lu Huaixi had been quiet, as though turning things over in her mind. Lost in thought, a commotion rose at the end of the lane, followed by the sound of approaching hooves and rolling wheels.

She hadn't yet had time to wonder whether it was perhaps one of the household's supply carts, when the driver's panicked shouting to rein in the horse reached her ears.

But the horse seemed to have been startled. It came charging forward.

Lu Huaixi's eyes went wide. She spun to step back—and in that instant, a hand caught her waist with swift precision.

She turned at the pull, shielding herself from being seen clearly. But the wheels churned up dust and grime as they passed, and it settled onto the swaying hem of her skirt.

The hand at her waist released almost immediately—so fleeting that, compared to the ruined dress, the touch was nearly forgettable.

"The carriage has stopped."

Xie Yuanjing glanced at the horse that had barely been reined in, then looked back. Noticing how close they had come to stand, he took a small step back.

"Are you all right?"

"Mm... but my dress is ruined. It was new. I was wearing it for the first time."

Lu Huaixi was even more unhappy now. The words came out soft and a little woeful.

A rare glimmer of something passed through Xie Yuanjing's normally expressionless dark eyes—the outer corners lifting slightly as he looked down at the hem.

"Later today, I'll have someone bring the Second Young Miss a new one."

"Ah—no, I didn't mean it like that."

Realizing the person standing before her was not one of her own family, Lu Huaixi quickly waved her hands in a fluster.

But Xie Yuanjing paid it no mind. He only met her mortified gaze, and let the tips of his fingers shift—just so.

"Whether you meant it that way or not, the responsibility is mine. I was the one who kept you here."

Then, without warning, he moved a few steps closer. He lowered his head—just slightly—confirming that the faint fragrance near the tip of his nose was not something he found unpleasant.

"So—are you willing to consider it? This marriage arrangement."

Seeing that Lu Huaixi didn't answer, he paused in thought, then added one more quiet, gentle line:

"If there's anything you're dissatisfied with, you can tell me."

chapters.title: Dissolution of Marriage After One Year
chapters.content:
When Lu Huaixi said nothing, she looked remarkably compliant.

Those dark eyes of hers shimmered with a liquid brightness, and when they met someone's gaze with that honest, open sincerity, it made it impossible to utter even one harsh word.

At that moment, her expression held a trace of confusion, a touch of bewilderment—yet she still remembered to sort through what she had just heard.

She didn't respond; Xie Yuanjing simply waited beside her without pressing. No extra expression crossed his face. He stood quietly at her outer side, as still as though they had always been standing here.

In honesty, the two of them standing together like this was a breach of propriety—and the timing of his proposal even more so, the kind of thing that should invite censure.

Yet Xie Yuanjing had spoken directly, and Lu Huaixi had listened with complete attention.

At some point, a carriage had turned into the lane and blocked them from view. Under the sound of its arrival, Lu Huaixi's thoughts cleared somewhat, and she met his gaze again.

"What if the Lu family can't give you what you need?"

Her brow was lightly creased, confusion still lingering—she had even forgotten the muddy hem of her skirt. "If your purpose isn't achieved, would this marriage suddenly be called off?"

"No."

Xie Yuanjing shook his head with a faint smile. "If things go smoothly, the wedding will come quickly—there won't be room for anything to change. And even if complications arise, what I've promised will not change."

He paused, as though a thought had crossed his mind, then added: "After the wedding, I won't restrict your going out."

Lu Huaixi startled, and didn't follow up on that.

Quickly, she asked again, uncertain: "Really—one year, and then a formal dissolution?"

Xie Yuanjing had "Mm" already at the back of his throat. But seeing her suddenly knit her brows in something conflicted, his words unexpectedly shifted course.

"If you think that's too short and might give rise to gossip, two years is also fine."

"Would it... would it not interfere with your—" She stopped. "Would it not cause any difficulty for you?"

Her brother's words—"someone in the marquis' household who's been waiting"—surfaced in Lu Huaixi's mind without warning.

She had asked without thinking, but partway through, she suddenly caught herself.

Setting aside whether this marriage would actually be arranged, even if it were—the two of them would only be playing out a performance, a matter of agreement and pretense.

Some things were fine to discuss. But other things, if raised, would only make her seem improper.

Lu Huaixi swallowed the rest of her question back down, and managed a somewhat sheepish smile toward Xie Yuanjing.

"It won't cause any difficulty."

As though he hadn't expected to hear anything like that, Xie Yuanjing paused for a moment. "I've never had any interest in marriage to begin with."

"Is that so."

Lu Huaixi tilted her head slightly—only then did she work up the boldness to look at him properly.

No interest. Well then, good.

In the carriage that had left earlier, the smell of liquor still lingered. He Jianxing slumped against the carriage wall, expression dark.

The rumor about Lu Huaixi possibly entering the palace was only half true. He wanted the Lu family's power to help him stand up against his eldest brother, but at this critical juncture, he could never risk taking Lu Huaixi as his wife.

Even though he did have feelings for her, what did that matter?

Once he had secured his future, he could still win her over.

It was just that he genuinely couldn't bear to give her up. If the two families hadn't suddenly fallen out, he should have been betrothed to her long ago.

"Young Master, this servant has never seen Second Young Miss Lu lose her temper before. Do you think she'll expose you for coming here?"

The servant beside him whispered with some worry.

Thinking of how their young master had arranged for the portrait to be sent over after hearing that someone had designs on Second Young Miss, the servant wasn't entirely sure what his master was after.

"And Young Master—didn't you already promise the Master that you'd marry that Miss Li from the Li family? If the Master finds out you came here..."

"Would she dare expose me?"

He Jianxing pressed his fingers to his temple and gritted out:

"No matter how scatterbrained she is, she ought to know that right now, I'm the only one willing to make her any promises. She's acting high and mighty because she hasn't grasped how dire her situation really is. Once she sees how thorny the palace business truly is, she'll understand who she needs to come begging to."

After a pause, He Jianxing continued: "Asking her to be a second wife is doing her a disservice, sure. But if she were sensible about it, wouldn't I give her the position of primary wife?"

"Young Master is absolutely right."

The servant nodded again and again. He Jianxing said nothing more.

He had come today not only to declare his feelings.

He had also wanted Lu Huaixi to remember his goodwill.

If she did enter the palace in the end, a girl with the Lu family's backing and that face of hers was bound to be favored.

And if she still thought of him from time to time, it would help him turn things around within the He family—a favorable outcome no matter what.

Lu Huaixi returned to her own courtyard.

That evening, someone sent things over: new garments, bolts of fabric, and a whole chest full of strange and delightful little trinkets.

The delivery was discreet—not a word left with the messenger. The things were quietly set before Lu Huaixi without even most of the household staff knowing.

The new dresses were lovely. The colors of the fabric were all the shades she typically liked to choose.

Lu Huaixi was still puzzling over how to return them when her gaze was drawn to the wooden chest beside them.

She let out a sound of surprise, completely forgetting to worry about whether her skirt would drag on the floor, and simply crouched down.

Inside were all manner of things. She had barely fished out a little clay figurine before she accidentally knocked over a small drum beside it. Then a celadon glazed porcelain duck caught her eye from the corner.

She reached deeper into the bottom, drew out a roly-poly toy, and set it on the floor—watching it sway back and forth.

Yaoshu leaned in for a closer look. When she saw what was inside, she couldn't help laughing out loud.

"Whoever sent these gifts to the young miss is treating her like a little child who needs cheering up."

"Hm?"

Lu Huaixi looked up at Yaoshu, still holding the glass bead she had just fished out. "What do you mean, treating a little child?"

"These little toys—I used to see people spoiling young children just like this. Everything the child could see from the street, all the little trinkets, all gathered up and brought home, so the child could pick out whatever she wanted to play with."

The room was lit with many lamps. Lu Huaixi tilted her head back, and the firelight fell directly into her eyes, bright enough to make her squint.

At Yaoshu's words, she immediately dropped what she was holding and stood up.

Whether it was from staring into the light too quickly, or from some dawning embarrassment she couldn't name, Lu Huaixi narrowed her eyes and, for once, turned away from Yaoshu's gaze.

"I'm not a little child."

"Of course not, miss."

Yaoshu nodded, coaxing her with a smile. "It's the one who sent the gifts who's treating you like a child. Next time you see him, miss, be sure to give him a piece of your mind."

Lu Huaixi had no idea what to say back, so she simply pressed her lips together and retreated obediently to the daybed—refusing to let herself look.

And at that very same hour, in Xie Yuanjing's residence, someone said the exact same thing.

"Are you proposing marriage—or raising a child?"

chapters.title: He's Not That Frightening, Actually
chapters.content:
The next day, it was nearly time for the morning meal when Lu Huaixi was still asleep.

The night before, she had spent a long time turning Xie Yuanjing's words over in her mind. And she had also found herself recalling the one time she had actually seen him.

At the riding grounds her brother had taken her to. That man had been in dark clothing too, and even the cloud motif on his belt was subdued.

Lu Huaixi had been ambling along on a small horse without a care in the world when his movement drew her gaze—and she followed his horse into the forest without quite realizing it.

But the man moved too quickly. By the time Lu Huaixi circled around and caught up, Xie Yuanjing had already dismounted and had his hand at someone's throat, as though he meant to snap it.

Lu Huaixi had been startled.

But then she saw the face of the person being seized—and the instinct to call for help was suppressed. That man was the most notorious wastrel in the capital. He deserved it. She wasn't about to interfere.

Still, she was frightened, and had been quietly trying to slip away when, without warning, Xie Yuanjing turned his head.

Sharp, cutting brows. Eyes that lifted and caught her through layers of shifting light and shadow—naturally fierce, radiating a barely-leashed menace.

Seen, and not at all troubled by it. He had met Lu Huaixi's gaze without flinching.

Hard to call arrogant, and yet—he was languid about it, and if she wasn't imagining it, the corner of his mouth had even curved up slightly.

But that day, Xie Yuanjing had not given her any trouble. Looking back on it afterward, Lu Huaixi thought: he was fierce, yes, but he hadn't truly gone too far.

The sun grew a little brighter, and the sleeping girl had just turned over when sounds came from outside.

"Miss, are you awake? The Old Master has sent someone to urge you along—he's waiting for you to join him for the morning meal."

Yaoshu sounded apologetic, not quite knowing how to wake her, but worried that if she waited any longer, they'd be late. "Nothing else is scheduled for today—why don't you come back and sleep afterward?"

Lu Huaixi opened her eyes in a daze, taking a long while to remember that she had promised her grandfather the night before she'd go over this morning.

She sat up. Her wide sleeping garment slid to one side, exposing snow-white skin and a delicate collarbone. Her eyes drooped, heavy with insufficient sleep, hiding some of her displeasure at being woken.

Yaoshu carried in warm water, then softly said a few more things.

Lu Huaixi didn't quite listen. She buried herself back into the soft pillow she was holding and closed her eyes again.

She always liked to hold something when she slept. Even in summer, she needed something within arm's reach.

"Where's Mother?"

"Madam and Young Master are already there. Master took leave from his duties today, so he's there as well. But the Old Madam is not."

"Is Second Aunt not there either?"

Lu Huaixi slowly gathered her wits. Her voice was slightly hoarse. She accepted the cup Yaoshu offered and drank a few sips before she began to properly wake.

"That's right. No one from the second branch is there."

The cup was set back down. In an instant, Lu Huaixi's expression shifted from confusion to understanding.

It must be to discuss her marriage.

But the marriage...

Lu Huaixi thought back to what she had been considering the night before.

Compared to being bound for a lifetime to some stranger, one year with Xie Yuanjing—and then a clean dissolution—was perhaps the more sensible option.

In the Jinhua courtyard, Lady Lu, née Liú Piǎorán, sat to one side, listening as the man at the head of the gathering spoke. Lu Yuanzhao was beside him, frowning in silence.

After a moment, Lady Liu lowered her eyes. Her voice held a firmness seldom heard from her.

"Father. Your daughter-in-law cannot agree to letting Xixi become entangled with the Chengen Marquis' household. Even if we must consider suitors, it should not be one from the marquis' household."

A pause, then Lady Liu continued: "My meaning is clear. No matter what the reason, Xixi's marriage must never be bound up with court politics. She shall only marry someone she herself wishes to marry."

The Old Master of the Lu family did not grow angry at that. Lu Yandao's expression only darkened slightly; he did not attempt to dissuade her.

"I would never sell my own granddaughter."

The Old Master had been injured some time ago. He had seemed mostly recovered, yet these past few days had visibly added to his exhaustion.

He sighed. The veteran official who had remained sharp and formidable at court now genuinely showed the signs of old age.

"Xixi's marriage—I had intended to find her a match myself. But given how things currently stand, how much time do you think we have to be careful about it?"

"Even so, we shouldn't push Xixi toward a fire pit! His Majesty's present attitude toward the Chengen Marquis is plain for all to see. And Xie Yuanjing clearly means to use the Lu family for his own ends. If they were to rush into an engagement now, His Majesty's displeasure would surely fall on Xixi as well!"

"But he can protect Xixi."

"Father—I'll take your word that he has the capacity to restore the marquis' household. But to say he can protect Xixi—"

"Yuanzhao, go outside."

The Old Master cut Lady Liu off, and waved the young man away.

Lu Yandao gave a nod as well.

"Go and see where your sister is—why hasn't she come yet?"

Though unwilling, Lu Yuanzhao had no choice but to rise.

The moment he was gone, the Old Master spoke directly:

"Our Lu family is not at peace either, as you well know. As for why Xixi's name ended up on that list—I imagine you've both formed your suspicions. If we continue letting her take her time finding a match, the outcome will only be that no one dares to step forward. And then even the last door left open to her will be sealed. Compared to that, a formal dissolution and a second marriage is no worse a path."

"But..."

"If Xixi truly entered the palace, the Lu family would spare no effort to ensure her safety. But the inner court has always been a place where dangers are impossible to fully guard against. No matter how far our reach extends, there will always be lapses. And beyond that—Xixi has only just come of age. How old is His Majesty? How old is she?"

The faces of everyone in the room changed. Lady Liu went pale, the color draining from her face all at once.

The Old Master gave her no time to dwell on it. His voice steady and deliberate, he pressed on:

"Now that the news has gotten out, no one will dare wade into these waters. The Xie family is indeed unsettled—but among all the talented young men in the capital, how many of them can match what Xie Yuanjing is capable of?"

"Father, your regard for Xie Yuanjing—is it because of that jade pendant?"

Lu Yandao frowned and picked up the thread, standing to one side.

Reluctant as he was to admit it, he understood their situation clearly. Xie Yuanjing was genuinely the most suitable option.

And precisely because the young man had his own purpose in this, he would not treat Xixi carelessly once they were wed.

The Old Master was silent for a moment, and did not deny it.

"The pendant is part of it."

He sighed, and said slowly: "Let us wait for Xixi to come first. If she is unwilling, we will find another way."

"Father, your son does not understand—why, because of that jade pendant—"

"That pendant is the Xie family's ancestral heirloom. His Majesty is not aware of this, but the late Emperor saw it once."

Lu Yandao froze, not quite grasping the implication.

But before he could ask again, the sound of a maidservant greeting someone drifted in from outside.

Lu Huaixi lifted the hem of her skirt and stepped into the room. Taking in the faces before her, her expression curved into a smile.

"Huaixi greets Grandfather, greets Father, greets Mother."

The faces around her softened at once—yet Lu Huaixi had still immediately sensed something was off.

Only when Grandfather mentioned Xie Yuanjing did she realize it was on her account.

"As for the Xie family—whether to agree or not is entirely your choice. Xie Yuanjing's methods can indeed be fierce, and if you are unwilling, your grandfather still has many former students. They may come from lesser families, but while your grandfather is still here, you will never be made to suffer for lack of money or standing."

Though it was all a performance, the formal dissolution would still be recorded with the authorities—a real and lasting document.

The Great Yu dynasty was open-minded and did not obstruct a woman's right to dissolve a marriage and remarry—but it would still invite talk, inevitably.

The Old Master finished speaking and let out another sigh. Lost in some thought she couldn't name, he suddenly broke into a fit of coughing.

Lu Huaixi startled, hurrying forward to pat his back.

Lady Liu still couldn't bear to let her daughter go, and was afraid Xixi—out of a sense of duty—wouldn't want to refuse the Old Master's words. She had been on the verge of speaking up for her.

But before she could open her mouth, she heard that soft, earnest voice:

"He's not that frightening, actually."

Lu Huaixi thought it over carefully, then smiled again. "Compared to being sent to the palace, I'd rather spend a year with him."

"Xixi?"

Lady Liu was caught off guard. She knitted her brows, clearly not in agreement.

"I mean it, Mother."

Lu Huaixi didn't hesitate. "I don't want to enter the palace, and I don't want to become a nun. I don't want to marry just anyone and spend my whole life managing the inner household of a stranger. And besides—"

She pressed her lips together, and the smile faded. The clear, guileless eyes that always held their honesty were touched, for the first time, by a glint of cold resolve.

"Besides—I want to find out who put my name on that list."

chapters.title: Used
chapters.content:
The engagement between the two families was settled quickly.

But at the Old Master's parting instruction, the matter was not made public. Not even the second branch of the Lu household was told.

When Shu Mama received word and prepared to put the portraits away, Lu Huaixi had them continue delivering the portraits to her courtyard, without giving any reason.

In the blink of an eye, ten days had passed.

Though the marriage had been arranged hastily and was mostly for appearances, the necessary preparations still needed to be made.

Lu Huaixi was still in something of a daze, yet she remembered she needed to go out and choose new fabric.

On the way, the carriage passed by Pei An Academy. She called for it to stop, intending to drop off several books for her brother.

The academy was unusually lively. Lu Huaixi almost thought she'd come to the wrong place, and was about to go around when she heard someone calling her name.

"Huaixi! What are you doing here?"

A young woman's voice carried a note of surprise. Then, as a few nearby faces turned to look, her tone suddenly brightened—joy artificially layered on top.

She walked over smiling and took Lu Huaixi's arm.

"I thought this kind of gathering wasn't to your taste, so when Sister Yu invited me the other day, I didn't mention it to you. If I'd known you'd stopped disliking these calligraphy-and-painting contests, I would've come with you."

Lu Huaixi looked at the speaker. It was Wu Wenlian, the concubine-born daughter of the Wu family—and also her friend, someone she had helped once before.

But before she could respond, Wu Wenlian pressed a hand over her mouth with a look of dismay, her eyes going careful and small.

"I didn't mean you dislike those things—don't be angry, Huaixi."

Someone else drifted closer, and noticing Lu Huaixi at what appeared to be a gathering of literary types, seemed faintly surprised.

But she wasn't as familiar with Lu Huaixi as Wu Wenlian was, and wary of her standing, kept her tone very deferential.

"I never thought I'd have the chance to meet Second Young Miss Lu—to think we'd cross paths at the Spring Harvest Gathering."

Hearing that somewhat ingratiating tone, Wu Wenlian's face dropped just a fraction—but only for an instant before she took Lu Huaixi's arm again.

"Yes, I didn't think Huaixi would come either."

She picked up the thread smoothly. "Today is the Spring Harvest Gathering—everyone writes poetry and paints without signing their names. Afterward, the three pieces most admired by the group are sent to Master Guo Shan for his comments. Since you're here, Huaixi, come join us."

Lu Huaixi had no taste for any of this. She waved it off and said plainly, "I can't do it. I don't like these things. I'm hopeless at them."

Wu Wenlian pulled her aside.

"If you don't want to take part in the judging, we'll just write for ourselves. It's a gathering of friends today too—a rare chance to meet. Come keep me company later and write something on my scroll. Afterward, when the gathering's over, I'll take it back and hang it up."

"But aren't you—"

"I have another scroll to enter in the judging. It won't matter."

Lu Huaixi knitted her brow.

Wu Wenlian was the quietest of their circle, and being born of a concubine, her conduct was always measured and acquiescent.

But the startled way she had called out earlier, and the warm insistence she was showing now—Lu Huaixi caught something she hadn't noticed before. Something off.

Even the excitement and expectation hidden in Wu Wenlian's voice felt off, though those should have been good emotions. Something about it just didn't sit right.

"I beg you, Huaixi. I don't have other interests like the others do—I'm not like Sister Xianya, who can ride horses and drink wine with you. You don't know how much I envy them for that. Huaixi—do you think you look down on my calligraphy?"

With things put that way, Lu Huaixi felt it would be harsh to refuse any further.

And it was true she'd been seeing less of Wu Wenlian lately—not out of any deliberate distance, just that she'd genuinely hadn't had the time.

"I never meant it like that. It's just that my handwriting is so unattractive, I was afraid it would spoil your painting."

"It won't—I don't care about things like that!"

With that, Wu Wenlian led her to a nearby pavilion. Inside, a scroll lay on the stone table, and a few other young women were standing around in clusters, chatting.

Not wanting to dampen the mood, Lu Huaixi picked up a brush and added a stroke of ink.

The title "beautiful simpleton" was no exaggeration—Lu Huaixi's handwriting was as ill-suited to praise as the poems she'd ever tried to compose.

But she herself had never been bothered by it. She never hid it, and never found it embarrassing.

Honestly, it wasn't her fault others commented on it.

Soon enough, Lu Huaixi's brush tip touched lightly onto the scroll.

Perhaps because Wu Wenlian's earlier reaction had been so strong, a few of the young women nearby had their attention drawn over and quietly gathered around.

Some recognized Lu Huaixi, and opened their eyes wide—waiting to see for themselves just how bad the "beautiful simpleton's" handwriting truly was.

Lu Huaixi paid them no mind. Her wrist lifted, and her brush moved, stroke by stroke, full-inked tip tracing one arc after another.

The pavilion, which had been softly lively, went suddenly quiet—then someone, unable to hold back, let out a soft laugh.

It wasn't ugly or misshapen. It was just... peculiar.

No girlish elegance or neat precision. No bold, sweeping freehand. No powerful, awe-inspiring force.

Only an exuberant roundness—each character thick and round and square at once, as if they'd been drawn rather than written, or scribbled for fun. A style entirely self-invented.

If something kind had to be said, you might just barely manage to call it "lively."

Lu Huaixi was not affected by the laughter. She kept her head down and carefully finished the final stroke.

Then she set the brush down and let out a quiet sigh.

Next to Wu Wenlian's work, her writing really was quite something to behold.

Just as she was thinking this, someone behind her spoke, amusement plain in the voice—and not recognizing Lu Huaixi:

"I hadn't noticed before, but looking now, Wenlian, your handwriting really has improved. I wonder if this sister of yours let her hand slip on purpose—to make your script look better by comparison and help you get selected?"

A brutal contrast. No wonder people made comparisons.

Lu Huaixi couldn't help laughing too—her brow curving—quite unbothered. "My writing's always like this. What a shame for this painting."

Seeing how easygoing she was about the teasing, several of the young women who didn't know her loosened up considerably.

But a few who did recognize her as Second Young Miss Lu were less warm.

"That handwriting—oh, it's Second Young Miss Lu's? Looking at it again, it's actually... quite a unique artistic conception."

"A shame about the painting, really. With that on it, how is anyone else supposed to compete? Acting out without any consideration—this is how you treat someone just because she's a concubine-born daughter who won't fight back. Some people."

"Exactly. A nice gathering, ruined by someone who just wants to be the center of attention. This is practically destroying someone's chances. And people say rumors about certain types aren't unfounded."

The comments ran both good and ill. But Lu Huaixi showed no reaction.

She lifted the scroll and looked at it for a moment, then turned her head toward Wu Wenlian, who had been silent throughout.

"Didn't you say you had another scroll to enter in the judging?"

Wu Wenlian's eyes had somehow gone red at their edges. Hearing Lu Huaixi's question, she raised her head, and managed a smile.

"It's fine. Whether it's judged or not doesn't matter."

"How can it not matter? She clearly ruined your painting."

Someone nearby seemed indignant on her behalf. "But at least this turned out to be a blessing in disguise—with this sister's bold brushwork as contrast, everyone can now see the quality of your calligraphy for themselves. If you just sent this scroll, Master Guo should certainly take notice."

The voice trailed off. Wu Wenlian fell silent again.

As though returning to how she usually was—more restrained, more awkward—she said nothing more about the other scroll she had mentioned preparing.

In that instant, Lu Huaixi finally understood where the wrongness she had sensed earlier had come from.

It was in the heart. A changed heart.

Amid everyone's remarks, Lu Huaixi—who had just put it together—suddenly smiled again.

She was beautifully made: her skin fair and soft, her eyes clear and bright as glass beads washed clean by rain, her lips a natural, delicate pink even without rouge—their faint press still holding a girlish quality not quite grown out of.

She raised her gaze toward Wu Wenlian.

When Xie Yuanjing came, he took a different path, skirting that part of the grounds.

Pei An Academy had two sections. This side was mostly where talented young men and women occasionally held their gatherings—sometimes very quiet, sometimes full of people.

Xie Yuanjing had never liked such things. He only came today because someone had recommended a scholar he wanted to meet.

Along the stone-paved path, a drift of laughter and voices could just be heard. Separated by a white wall, they came through clearly.

He was about to step onto the covered walkway and leave, when a name—now somewhat familiar to him—drifted over.

"Was that Second Young Miss Lu just now?"

A young woman's voice, puzzled. "She's here, she's here—why are people saying things about her? Just because her handwriting is bad?"

Xie Yuanjing's step paused. To the surprise of the guard behind him, he stood there and listened for a few exchanges.

After a moment, he gave a quiet, low laugh.

The little girl had been used.

Thinking of how she was now, in some sense, his own person, he turned around without much hesitation.

chapters.title: Another Side of the Girl
chapters.content:
Lu Huaixi looked at Wu Wenlian, the scroll she'd written on still in her hand, entirely indifferent to anyone's comparisons.

She waited—as though expecting some kind of reply. But Wu Wenlian said nothing.

She didn't speak up for Lu Huaixi, and didn't explain herself either. Just stood there, silent.

"You've seen my handwriting before, Wenlian."

Lu Huaixi wasn't accusing her. Her voice was calm—her eyes even curved slightly, as if retrieving a memory.

"When you were being bullied, you stayed at our house for half a month. During those two weeks, you came with me to the tutor's classes, and you saw me practice my calligraphy."

"I..."

"And just now, it was you who asked me to come write something alongside you. Everyone in the capital knows I hate these things."

Wu Wenlian went quiet again, her head dropping.

"If you wanted to enter this scroll in the judging, you never should have brought me over to write on it."

A pause. Then Lu Huaixi said: "I thought we were friends."

Those words landed heavy.

There was much more Lu Huaixi could have said. She had many ways of dismantling Wu Wenlian's position right there if she'd wanted to.

But it would have been tiresome.

She also understood clearly that the women echoing in with criticism weren't truly invested in whether the characters on this scroll were ugly or not.

"Huaixi, I didn't mean it like that. I—I wasn't thinking clearly just now..."

"Then what did you mean?"

Wu Wenlian hadn't expected her to bring up the time she had spent at the Lu household.

She didn't want to be humiliated, and her words came out tangled in confusion.

But if Lu Huaixi hadn't appeared out of nowhere, hadn't suddenly drawn away all the attention that had been on her—she wouldn't have had this idea. Wouldn't have wanted to embarrass her.

She wasn't satisfied with that.

"I hadn't seen you in a while, and I thought—thought maybe you'd practiced your calligraphy."

Having said it, Wu Wenlian's hidden hand tightened in her sleeve.

This Spring Harvest Gathering had been something she had waited a long time for and prepared for carefully.

She had been sure Lu Huaixi wouldn't come—sure that Lu Huaixi's face wouldn't steal her moment. She had waited and hoped, and in the end, still been overshadowed.

"Sorry. If I had known—"

"Interesting writing. Rather charming, actually."

A voice came from some distance away, cutting through Wu Wenlian's words.

Everyone startled, turning to look at who had spoken.

Xie Yuanjing had not come too close. He stopped at a slight distance, his gaze settling briefly on the scroll in Lu Huaixi's hand.

After his words fell, those nearby went briefly silent—then turned in unison to look again at those striking characters.

Only Lu Huaixi looked up and met the speaker's eyes.

The two of them hadn't seen each other since the engagement was set. The last time she hadn't thought much of it, but now that there was something between them—even knowing it was a pretense—an inexplicable unease stirred in Lu Huaixi.

But she wasn't someone who liked to be coy.

The unfamiliar feeling flickered and passed, and she turned her clear, bright eyes on him.

That expression—carrying a trace of grievance, yet not quite believing she'd been praised—drew a curve to Xie Yuanjing's lips before he had time to think about it. A second smile today, surfacing out of nowhere.

It was brief, but those nearby had caught it plainly.

"Quite distinctive—is this Second Young Miss Lu's writing?"

"Yes. These few lines."

Xie Yuanjing glanced back at the scroll and gave a nod, then said, with the air of complimenting a small child: "Rare to see a script so peculiar yet containing such depth. If you have a moment to spare, would you mind writing a piece for me?"

Saying something outlandish with complete composure left those who heard it unable to tell if he meant it. Blank-faced bewilderment spread around the pavilion.

But few there didn't recognize Xie Yuanjing.

And thinking of his background, they all remembered: this eldest young lord of the Chengen Marquis' household had studied under the great master Cao Gong. His calligraphy and painting both ranked first in the capital.

If he called it interesting, then interesting it was.

Those who had been angling to pick at the characters fell quietly silent, stepped back, and pretended nothing had happened.

The surroundings settled, and Lu Huaixi had no intention of staying longer.

As she turned to go, Wu Wenlian called out to her.

"Huaixi, I..."

Face flushed, she glanced once toward the man standing in the distance, then pulled her gaze back, her voice barely above a whisper. "I didn't mean it earlier—"

"It doesn't matter."

Lu Huaixi waved it off, expression easy. "I won't bring up what happened before. But going forward, there's no need for us to keep in contact."

Wu Wenlian's fingers dug tightly into her sleeve. She watched Lu Huaixi turn away freely, heading toward the man who had spoken up for her, resentment welling up in her chest—complicated and unwilling.

"Lu Huaixi—have you always looked down on me?"

Lu Huaixi's steps paused.

She turned her head slightly. The sunlight traced the line of her cheek like a perfect brushstroke.

"Every time we gathered, it was always you and Zhou Xianya talking so much—whenever I was there, the way you looked at me always carried pity. And the things you sent me were always plain and unassuming. You said we were friends, but you never really treated me as one, did you?"

Wu Wenlian's voice trembled slightly, like grievances held too long finally spilling over.

"Everything you gave me was charity—to feed that high and mighty kindness of yours. You looked down on me for being born of a concubine. All the years we've known each other, you never once mentioned you had this kind of backing. You never had any real heart for me as a friend. Never."

In all the years she had known Wu Wenlian, Lu Huaixi's conscience had been clear.

Being accused like this was something she had never imagined.

She wavered for a beat, then truly began to think—wondering if she had done something wrong somewhere.

But the silence lasted only a moment.

Quickly, Lu Huaixi met her gaze. Her expression was steady.

"Backing—meaning Xie Yuanjing?"

She said earnestly: "Even if he hadn't happened to see this today, I would've been fine. Everyone here is from a respected family—they could see through your intentions. The ones who went along with it just wanted an excuse."

Lu Huaixi's eyes let the light in, looking at someone as if she could see straight through to their heart.

She had no great surge of emotion. Compared to Wu Wenlian, whose composure had completely unraveled, she spoke as though discussing something that had nothing to do with her.

"As for the charity you mentioned—anything I've sent you before, if you think it wasn't worth your time, you're welcome to throw it away."

"Lu Huaixi—what right do you have to be so unbothered by this?"

The one who had been called to a stop faltered for a moment. Her soft lips parted, then she lowered her eyes, swallowing down that knot of something she didn't want to say more about.

"Wenlian, you and I haven't known each other for such a short time. We may not be able to be friends—but let's not make it ugly."

She had chosen her gifts with care, and been called careless. She had strategized on her behalf—and been told it was condescension.

She had kept her gifts low-key precisely so Wenlian wouldn't draw attention in the Wu household. And she had been called unthoughtful.

Even Zhou Xianya had complained once, saying Lu Huaixi gave Wu Wenlian too much of her attention.

Hearing all of this now—even with Lu Huaixi's somewhat sluggish sensitivity to negative feelings—she couldn't help but feel a sting.

She didn't look at Wu Wenlian again. She turned away without hesitation and walked out of her line of sight.

Xie Yuanjing hadn't left. He watched Lu Huaixi hold in what was clearly a barely-suppressed hurt, let go cleanly and decisively—and found he couldn't look away.

A side of this girl he hadn't expected to see.

"What are you thinking about?"

chapters.title: Coaxing a Child
chapters.content:
Outside the academy, Xie Yuanjing's voice sounded at just the right moment, pulling Lu Huaixi back from the dark place her thoughts had been sinking toward.

Lu Huaixi looked up. Only then did she remember she still hadn't thanked him for earlier.

"I was thinking about the books my brother asked me to send. I forgot to deliver them."

"My man is heading inside just now to find someone. Hand over the books and I'll have him deliver them at the same time."

Lu Huaixi had no wish to speak about what had just happened, and Xie Yuanjing didn't bring it up either—he simply had someone take the books.

The guard behind them moved quickly, keeping his eyes down, yet had committed to memory every detail: the fleeting smile on his master's face and the absurdly composed appraisal he'd just offered.

"About what happened just now—thank you. But—"

Lu Huaixi looked at him. "The things you said earlier—you were making it up, weren't you?"

She pressed her lips together, a little hesitant. "You were standing so far away that you couldn't actually see my writing clearly, could you?"

Xie Yuanjing gave a quiet laugh—not denying it, and not answering right away either.

He hadn't intended to get involved in any of it. But since this little girl had more or less bound herself to him, and he had heard it, it wouldn't have done not to step in.

Besides, he was six years her senior. If they were on the same ship, it was only natural he should take up the responsibility of an elder brother.

Coaxing a child was nothing at all.

"You're right, I couldn't see it clearly."

"All right then."

Lu Huaixi nodded. Exactly as she'd expected.

She knew her writing wasn't good—she'd always known, and had never tried to hide it.

"I didn't like studying when I was little, and I didn't like practicing calligraphy either. Going forward... I probably still won't."

"Mm. I may not have seen clearly, but I know what your writing is like."

Xie Yuanjing looked back at the path ahead, keeping a measured distance as they walked. He said, lightly:

"What I said was no lie."

"?"

"I did mean it's interesting. It's not ugly. And I do want you to write a piece for me when you have time."

They had soon reached the place where the carriages waited.

His voice was low and unhurried, carrying that languid quality of his—but his gaze, as it met hers, held not a trace of insincerity.

"Where are you headed? I'll have two of my men go with you."

"That's all right."

Lu Huaixi shook her head quickly. "Just browsing, picking up a few things."

Thinking of why she had come out today, she couldn't say it aloud. The tips of her ears went red before she even tried.

Xie Yuanjing was watching her. He saw the flush creep across fair skin—bit by bit, then spreading—and inexplicably thought he hadn't had quite enough of his afternoon tea.

Noticing her awkwardness, he saw no reason to press.

He gave a small nod.

"All right."

After leaving the academy, Lu Huaixi sat in the carriage looking glum.

The low, quiet feelings she hadn't wanted to show in front of everyone—now that she was away from it—could no longer quite be held back.

If Xie Yuanjing hadn't been there to pull some of her focus, she'd probably have let herself cry.

That kind of mood didn't lend itself to choosing new clothes.

Thinking that the wedding was not far off, Lu Huaixi simply told the driver to change course—and made a quiet trip to Shun'an Lane.

Everyone in the capital knew that the Lu family's second daughter didn't like reading and had a head full of nothing. What few people knew was that she had something she loved—dancing.

As for how good she was—

There was a woman in the capital called Chengyue. She had never shown her face, but the dances she had choreographed—performed by the most skilled dancers in the city, taught to the ladies in the inner palace—were known to all.

Those who speculated about Chengyue assumed she must be getting on in years, well past thirty. Little did they know she had only just turned half that age.

Beyond that, Lu Huaixi also loved to sing, and had become an accomplished qin player as a result.

But these things were difficult to display openly. A head mistress of a household couldn't very well be known as a woman of exceptional dance or extraordinary singing.

She didn't mind for herself, and had even used her own saved-up silver to take in a group of performers who had no other prospects.

But she imagined her future husband would mind.

So it was better not to marry at all.

Yet saying that was rather late now.

In one month, the wedding would take place—pretense though it was. And in this one year, going out to teach dance or to sing was, after all, not quite appropriate.

After the carriage stopped, Lu Huaixi slipped in through the back door.

From inside came the sounds of strings and flutes drifting on the wind, occasionally laced with women's laughter.

Lu Huaixi was usually very eager—a short walk would have been nothing—but knowing she was coming to say goodbye for a while, her feet slowed all on their own.

"Xixi?"

The woman who managed the place spotted her and came over smiling.

The women here earned their living through performance, not through any other means. Though only two people here knew Lu Huaixi's true identity, everyone in the place was warm toward her.

Pretty girls—nobody disliked them.

Especially one so gentle and sweet, who didn't look down on their station.

"What brought you here so suddenly—did you think of a new dance for someone to learn?"

chapters.title: Sending Her a Calligraphy Copybook
chapters.content:
The woman's name was Qing Ling, and she was one of the two people who knew Lu Huaixi's true identity.

Her smile was graceful and gentle, but the moment she stepped close and saw the look on Lu Huaixi's face, the smile stilled at the corner of her mouth. "What happened? Where did you get hurt?"

Lu Huaixi was, by all rights, their benefactress—yet her young age and pure heart had always made everyone treat her more like a little sister.

Seeing the redness around her eyes and the frown she was wearing, Qing Ling's own brow creased in sympathy.

"Nothing happened. I just came to—"

The words cut off before she could finish. From somewhere ahead in the main hall, a sudden burst of noise broke out.

Then came a wave of harsh shouting—sharp and cutting—layered over a woman's sobbing and struggling.

Several faces changed at once. Without a second thought, Qing Ling pulled Lu Huaixi into a nearby side room.

"Don't get involved in this kind of thing—and don't let yourself be seen. It looks like some kind of misunderstanding—I'll go take a look."

Lu Huaixi opened her mouth, then closed it and nodded.

There were occasional troublemakers here. And although the women of the place made their living from performance and nothing else, people always assumed the worst.

Lu Huaixi waited. Nearly half an hour later, Qing Ling came back from the front, expression dark.

"What happened?"

"Someone caused a scene."

Qing Ling frowned.

"A new girl who came recently—her family couldn't make ends meet. Her parents had wanted to sell her off, but she wanted to learn to dance, so she came here of her own accord. I saw she was young and had a natural gift for it, so I kept her. A few days ago she danced out front for the first time—and someone set their eyes on her."

Knowing the person before her was only fifteen or sixteen, Qing Ling kept her words simple.

But Lu Huaixi understood perfectly well what "set their eyes on her" meant.

"The hall has guards, doesn't it? Is it a matter of not enough money—too few people hired?"

"The ones we brought in are fine against drunken troublemakers and ruffians—but when a woman comes to cause a scene, the men don't dare step in."

A pause, then Qing Ling added: "She won't go and manage her own household, and instead comes here to bully a girl with no one to turn to."

"And the girl—how is she now?"

"Couldn't get away. Took a beating from the woman. Nearly had her face scratched up too."

Lu Huaixi felt the words jam somewhere in her throat.

Today had given her too many silences—first the low ache of sorrow, and now this: dejection and a weary kind of helplessness.

When she had first put money into this place, it wasn't only because she loved dancing and singing—it was also because many of the girls here had come from poverty.

Other places had turned them away. Lu Huaixi had thought: then she would take them in.

But she had thought it through too simply.

Without Qing Ling, she doubted she could have kept this place standing.

"She probably won't want to stay now, will she?"

"Not at all."

At that, Qing Ling's expression lifted slightly.

"She's a stubborn one—crying and saying she won't leave. Still says she refuses to believe dancing is something to be ashamed of. Oh—and the girl said that one day, when she's good enough, she wants to dance to the Chengyue's choreography."

Being Chengyue herself, Lu Huaixi was momentarily taken aback.

"Never mind her for now—today's business still needs to be settled. If I don't do right by her, not only did the girl suffer for nothing, but everyone else will think this place really is something shameful."

Qing Ling poured Lu Huaixi a cup of tea as she spoke.

"But first—what about our little Xixi? What brings you by today? A new dance you thought of for someone to perform? Or something else to arrange?"

Remembering why she had come, Lu Huaixi couldn't bring herself to say the words: I may not be able to come regularly for a while.

Something seemed to straighten out the hesitation in her heart, reminding her of all the difficulty she had gone through for the things she loved.

After a long moment, she lowered her eyes and made a new decision.

"I just came to see you, Sister."

Lu Huaixi smiled and said, "I may not be able to come as often for the next few months—I was afraid Qing Ling might think I'd run off, so I came to tell you."

She paused, then added: "If anything happens here, Sister Qing Ling, send word to Yaoshu."

She hadn't decided yet whether to tell Xie Yuanjing. And she wasn't sure how he would react if she did—whether he'd still let her leave the house.

Her instinct was that he probably wouldn't.
